steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on getting text-to-image models to handle explicit spatial relations (left of, below, etc.) by fine-tuning them on an automatically derived dataset. Explain the problem, why we think the training data is to blame, what we built and how we evaluate it, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Text-to-image generators and their weakness with explicit spatial relations
2. Hypothesis: training data lacks spatial relations (LAION-2B analysis)
3. Approach: synthetic spatial captions for real images (SR4G)
4. Fine-tuning and evaluation
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Text-to-image generators and spatial relations
- Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Dalle-3: rapid advances, lots of interest
- still far from perfect, important weaknesses
- prior work: do not represent explicit spatial relations well (left of, below)
- limits applications like text-based image editing

2. Hypothesis: lack of spatial relations in training data
- analysed LAION-2B (used to train Stable Diffusion, state-of-the-art open source)
- captions = alt-text fields of web images
- automatic search for spatial words (left, right, below...): only 0.72\% of captions
- 64.1\% of these are left/right -> not learnable, random horizontal flips in training

3. Approach: focus on training data
- improve end-to-end diffusion models via data; complementary to architectural modifications
- automatically generate synthetic captions with explicit spatial relations, paired with real images
- COCO object annotations + heuristic rules on two bounding boxes
- dataset: Spatial Relations for Generation (SR4G)

4. Fine-tuning and evaluation
- fine-tune two Stable Diffusion models on SR4G
- assumption: exposure to spatial image-caption pairs improves representing relations
- VISOR metric (recent), extended to more relations; compare against unmodified base models

5. Contributions
- (1) release SR4G: first benchmark to fine-tune/develop/evaluate spatial understanding, 14 explicit relations
- (2) fine-tuning on SR4G improves spatial understanding, more accurate images
- (3) holds on unseen objects -> models learn relations, generalize
- (4) beats state-of-the-art in spatial understanding with fewer parameters, no complex architectures or LLMs

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Text-to-image generators like Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and Dalle-3 have advanced a lot recently and there is a lot of interest in them. But these systems are still not perfect and they have some important weaknesses. One of them is that current text-to-image generators don't represent explicit spatial relations like left of or below very well, as several studies have observed, and this limits what they can do in important applications such as text-based image editing.

Our hypothesis is that the bad performance on explicit spatial relations comes from the training datasets of these models not having such relations. To check this we analysed the LAION-2B dataset, which was used to train Stable Diffusion, the state-of-the-art open source model. The captions in LAION-2B come from the alt-text fields of images on the web. We searched automatically for explicit spatial relations (left, right, below and so on) and only 0.72\% of the captions contain the target words. Also, 64.1\% of these relations are left and right, and image generators cannot capture these anyway, because random horizontal flips are applied to the images during training.

Approach: focus on training data
- improve end-to-end diffusion models via data; complementary to architectural modifications
- automatically generate synthetic captions with explicit spatial relations, paired with real images
- COCO object annotations + heuristic rules on two bounding boxes
- dataset: Spatial Relations for Generation (SR4G)

Fine-tuning and evaluation
- fine-tune two Stable Diffusion models on SR4G
- assumption: exposure to spatial image-caption pairs improves representing relations
- VISOR metric (recent), extended to more relations; compare against unmodified base models

Contributions
- (1) release SR4G: first benchmark to fine-tune/develop/evaluate spatial understanding, 14 explicit relations
- (2) fine-tuning on SR4G improves spatial understanding, more accurate images
- (3) holds on unseen objects -> models learn relations, generalize
- (4) beats state-of-the-art in spatial understanding with fewer parameters, no complex architectures or LLMs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Text-to-image generators like Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and Dalle-3 have advanced a lot recently and there is a lot of interest in them. But these systems are still not perfect and they have some important weaknesses. One of them is that current text-to-image generators don't represent explicit spatial relations like left of or below very well, as several studies have observed, and this limits what they can do in important applications such as text-based image editing.

Our hypothesis is that the bad performance on explicit spatial relations comes from the training datasets of these models not having such relations. To check this we analysed the LAION-2B dataset, which was used to train Stable Diffusion, the state-of-the-art open source model. The captions in LAION-2B come from the alt-text fields of images on the web. We searched automatically for explicit spatial relations (left, right, below and so on) and only 0.72\% of the captions contain the target words. Also, 64.1\% of these relations are left and right, and image generators cannot capture these anyway, because random horizontal flips are applied to the images during training.

Because there are so few captions with spatial relations, we focus on the training data in order to improve current end-to-end diffusion models. This is complementary to the architectural modifications to the system itself that have been proposed. More concretely, we propose an approach that automatically generates synthetic captions with explicit spatial relations, paired with real images. We use the object annotations in COCO and heuristic rules that infer the spatial relation between two bounding boxes, and with these we build a dataset of real images with synthetic captions, which we call Spatial Relations for Generation (SR4G).

We then fine-tune two Stable Diffusion models on SR4G. The assumption is that if the models see image-caption pairs with explicit spatial relations, they will get better at representing those relations. To evaluate the fine-tuned models and compare them to the unmodified base models we use the VISOR metric, which was proposed recently, and we extend it so it supports more spatial relations.

The contributions of this paper are: (1) we release SR4G, the first benchmark for fine-tuning, developing and evaluating the spatial understanding capabilities of text-to-image models, with 14 explicit relations; (2) our experiments show that fine-tuning Stable Diffusion on SR4G improves its understanding of spatial relations and gives more accurate images; (3) the improvement also holds when testing on unseen objects, which shows that the models learn the relations and generalize to unseen objects; (4) the results are better than the state-of-the-art in spatial understanding for image generation, with fewer parameters and without complex architectures or Large Language Models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Text-to-image generators such as Midjourney, Stable Diffusion [1] and Dalle-3 [2] have recently made rapid advances and attracted a lot of interest. However, these systems are still far from perfect and show some important weaknesses. For instance, as observed by [3] and [4] among others, current text-to-image generators do not represent explicit spatial relations like left of or below well, which limits their capabilities for important applications such as text-based image editing [5].

We hypothesize that the poor performance for explicit spatial relations is due to the lack of such relations in the datasets used to train these models. To support our hypothesis we analysed the LAION-2B dataset [6], which has been used to train the state-of-the-art open source model Stable Diffusion. LAION-2B takes its captions from the alt-text fields of images on the web. We automatically searched for explicit spatial relations (left, right, below and so on) and found that only 0.72\% of captions contain the target words. Furthermore, 64.1\% of these relations are left and right, which image generators cannot capture, since random horizontal flips are applied to images during training.

Motivated by the lack of captions with spatial relations, we focus on the training data to improve current end-to-end diffusion models; this is complementary to the architectural modifications proposed for the system itself [4,7]. More concretely, we propose an approach to automatically generate synthetic captions containing explicit spatial relations, paired with real images. Leveraging the object annotations in COCO [8] and heuristic rules that infer the spatial relation between two bounding boxes, we build a dataset of real images paired with synthetic captions, called Spatial Relations for Generation (SR4G).

We use SR4G to fine-tune two Stable Diffusion models, assuming that exposure to image-caption pairs with explicit spatial relations will enhance the ability of the models to represent those relations. To evaluate our fine-tuned models and compare them to the unmodified base models, we use the recently proposed VISOR metric [3], which we extend to support more spatial relations.

The contributions of this paper are the following: (1) We release SR4G, the first benchmark that allows to fine-tune, develop and evaluate the spatial understanding capabilities of text-to-image models for 14 explicit relations; (2) Our experiments show that fine-tuning Stable Diffusion on SR4G improves the understanding of spatial relations and yields more accurate images; (3) The improvement holds even when tested on unseen objects, showing that the models learn the relations and generalize to unseen objects; (4) The results exceed the state-of-the-art in spatial understanding for image generation [4,7] with fewer parameters, avoiding complex architectures or Large Language Models.
